title: AI Now Drives Three in Four Finance Teams, but Data Quality Threatens to Stall the Gains
excerpt: A KPMG survey of over 1,000 senior finance leaders across 20 countries found that AI adoption has more than doubled since 2024, but only 42% of organizations are prepared to audit their AI-driven financial processes.
body:
• Active AI use in finance has more than doubled from 30% in 2024 to 75% in 2026, according to a KPMG survey of 1,013 senior finance leaders across 20 countries
  • Organizations deploying agentic AI report 32 percentage points stronger performance on average, rising to nearly 40 points on forecast accuracy and ROI
  • Only 42% of organizations are assurance-ready for AI-enabled finance processes, and just 23% say AI is exceeding expectations
  • Data quality is cited by 36% of organizations as both the top barrier and top opportunity for extracting more value from AI

Artificial intelligence has crossed the threshold from experimentation to daily use in corporate finance departments worldwide, but data quality and governance are emerging as the critical barriers separating leaders from laggards, according to a major new KPMG report.

The "Global AI in Finance 2026" survey, based on responses from 1,013 senior finance leaders across 20 countries and 13 sectors, found that active AI use in finance functions has more than doubled in two years — rising from 30% in 2024 to 75% in 2026. Nearly three-quarters of leaders said AI is meeting or exceeding return-on-investment expectations.

Decision Engine, Not Cost Lever

The most significant finding is where AI is delivering the strongest gains. Rather than automating routine transactions, AI is making its biggest impact in judgment-heavy areas where finance teams have historically been weakest.

Seventy percent of organizations reported improvements in decision-making quality, 71% said decisions were being made faster, and 64% reported better forecasting accuracy over the past year, according to the survey.

Organizations that have deployed agentic AI — systems that can plan, reason, and act autonomously — are pulling away from the pack. Those at the orchestrating and multi-agent stages outperformed organizations still in early planning by 32 percentage points on average, and by nearly 40 points on forecast accuracy and ROI specifically.

The Assurance Gap

Adoption alone is not translating into exceptional results for most organizations. While 71% said AI is meeting expectations, only 23% said it is exceeding them — a narrower group than the headline satisfaction figure suggests.

The differentiator, according to KPMG, is governance. Organizations that can demonstrate at any time how AI-driven results were generated reported significant improvements three to six times more frequently than those without such capabilities. Thirty-three percent of assurance-ready organizations reported significantly fewer errors, compared with just 6% of those that were not.

Yet only 42% of organizations surveyed were strongly assurance-ready for AI-enabled finance processes. A mere 29% systematically track where their AI applications fail.

Data Quality: The Universal Constraint

Thirty-six percent of organizations identified improving data quality, integration, and system interoperability as their greatest opportunity to extract more value from AI — making it both the most cited barrier and the most cited opportunity in the survey.

Performance varied sharply by sector. In banking, 71% of leaders reported moderate or significant improvements in forecast accuracy. In healthcare, that figure dropped to 44% — a 27-point gap that KPMG attributed to differences in data foundations. Banking benefits from structured, standardized data sets that give AI models a strong foundation. Healthcare faces fragmented, unstructured data sources that limit what AI can deliver.

Workforce Implications

On the talent front, 38% of organizations said they are upskilling existing finance teams to work alongside AI, but only 28% are rethinking the types of talent they need. KPMG noted that the gap between training people to use AI tools and building a comprehensive human-AI workforce model has not yet closed.

For Indian-origin finance professionals and technology leaders — many of whom are at the forefront of AI deployment at global banks and technology companies — the findings offer a clear signal. The competitive advantage in AI is shifting from adoption speed to operational maturity: governance, controls, measurement, and data foundations will determine which organizations convert AI spending into durable performance gains.
